title: Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984)
shortTitle: Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984)
summary: The historical Chevron framework required acceptance of a permissible agency construction when Congress had left the relevant question unresolved. Loper Bright later overruled that interpretive methodology while preserving ordinary statutory stare decisis for earlier holdings.

sections.Parties: The Natural Resources Defense Council challenged an Environmental Protection Agency regulation permitting a plantwide definition of a stationary source under the Clean Air Act. Chevron appears as the named petitioner in the Supreme Court litigation. The assigned historical account explains EPA’s rule and the challenge, but does not provide the complete list of participating industrial and governmental parties. (Printed 933.)
sections.Material Facts:
The Clean Air Act Amendments of 1977 required states that had not achieved national air-quality standards to impose permit requirements on new or modified major stationary sources. Those permits carried stringent conditions. EPA’s 1981 regulation allowed a state to treat pollution-emitting activities within a commonly controlled industrial grouping on contiguous or adjacent properties as one source. The plant could then install or modify a device without triggering those conditions if its total emissions did not increase. (Printed 933.)

That plantwide “bubble” mattered because different definitions of source changed which modifications required permits. EPA had changed its approach over time, and the statute’s history did not establish a single stable congressional policy defining a source as either the entire plant or each component. (Printed 933–934.)
sections.Procedural History: The D.C. Circuit set aside the regulation. Its opinion, written by then-Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg, relied on circuit precedent restricting use of the bubble concept. The Supreme Court reversed, concluding that the lower court had improperly fixed a judicial definition after finding that Congress had not required it. The casebook presents the decision as the origin of the later Chevron era and notes that three Justices did not participate. (Printed 933, 935.)
sections.Issue: Did the Clean Air Act permit EPA to define stationary source on a plantwide basis for the nonattainment permitting program, and how should a reviewing court proceed when Congress had not resolved that precise interpretive question? (Printed 933–934.)
sections.Holding: The Court upheld EPA’s interpretation as a reasonable accommodation of competing statutory policies and reversed the judgment setting the rule aside. The framework later associated with Chevron asked first whether Congress had directly resolved the precise issue using traditional interpretive tools. If so, that answer controlled. If the statute remained silent or ambiguous on the issue, the court asked whether the agency’s interpretation was permissible; it did not require the agency’s reading to be the one the court independently preferred. This is the historical methodology overruled in Loper Bright. (Printed 933–935; 952–953.)
sections.Reasoning:
The Court examined statutory and regulatory history and found no congressional commitment to one definition of source. EPA’s interpretation accommodated pollution control and other regulatory interests within a technical, complex scheme. The agency’s detailed consideration, substantive expertise, and connection to a politically accountable executive supported allowing it to make the policy choice. A change from an earlier agency view did not alone defeat deference, because the agency could reconsider the program as experience and policy changed. (Printed 934–935.)

The opinion distinguished express delegations to fill statutory gaps from delegations understood as implicit. Under the ensuing doctrine, both could justify a range of reasonable agency choices. The court nevertheless retained authority to reject an interpretation contrary to clear congressional intent. The casebook cautions that the opinion’s lengthy substantive analysis and its later reception make the familiar two-step formulation a historical development, rather than a complete description of every sentence of Chevron itself. It also identifies later restrictions and extensions in Mead, Brand X, King v. Burwell, and City of Arlington. (Printed 934–938.)
